what: The Chefs’ Warehouse distributes specialty food products to restaurants: high-end meats, seafood, cheeses, produce, oils and pastries, as well as everyday ingredients. It serves chefs in major US cities, Canada and the Middle East.
customers: Independent fine-dining and upscale casual restaurants, hotels, country clubs and caterers.
moat: A focus on chefs who value quality over price, a broad catalogue of specialty products and knowledgeable sales staff. Larger distributors like Sysco serve chains better than fine dining.
risks: Margins are thin, like all food distribution, and depend on restaurant traffic.
Fine dining is sensitive to economic downturns.
Growth has come partly from acquisitions.
opportunities: Revenue grew from $1.7B in 2021 to $4.5B over the last twelve months.
Net income rose from a small loss in 2021 to $102M over the last twelve months.
Free cash flow is now consistently positive.
Nine analysts average a target of $118, about 12% above the price.
watch: Restaurant traffic in its key cities and gross margin.
view: Chefs’ Warehouse has executed well: revenue more than doubled since 2021, margins rose and free cash flow turned consistently positive. It owns a niche the big distributors serve badly, fine-dining and upscale restaurants that want specialty products and service.

The market has noticed: at 45 times trailing earnings and 39 times forward, the shares are priced as a growth company. That is a high multiple for a distributor whose customers are among the first to suffer in a recession.

This turns on restaurant spending holding up. I think the business is good and getting better, but the valuation leaves no room for a slowdown. I would call it fully priced and wait for a better entry.
bull: Fine dining keeps growing and margins expand further.
bear: A consumer slowdown hits upscale restaurants and the high multiple contracts.
